title: Should Emergencies Be More Social?
html:
In both sudden onset and protracted emergencies that I have responded to, I have regularly found that getting organizations (or the people in them) to share information is a major hurdle. In international emergencies, sector-based groups struggle to collect information from their members and the inter-sector groups (like UNOCHA in an international emergency) struggle to collect from these sector-based groups for high level analysis. Beyond trying to convince individuals of the benefit of sharing, delivering value-added products, and setting globally agreed policy, I have seen a variety of tricks used to entice information sharing: controlling access to UN-HAS flights, holding the only key to toilets, and determining if your organization can apply for emergency funds in the crisis. In the past, we also had Humanitarian Information Centres (HIC) which provided information management services, such as Internet access and map creation, to the humanitarian community in order to attract people to stop by and share their data. By leaving their data, they got a map in return which was a hugely valuable service 3-5+ years ago as such work required specialized skills and software.

But, as we enter an era where organizations have much better Internet connection in emergencies and they can either create their own maps online or turn to amazing groups like the Digital Humanitarian Network, it means that responders do not need to leave their office/team to visit a central physical centre to request help. 

Over the past couple of years, I have been telling humanitarians that we still need a centre, but that I wanted added services. I talked about providing lightning speed Internet, serving high quality coffee (perhaps through a partnership with a company like Starbucks), facilitating support from remote groups like the Digital  Humanitarian Network, hosting regular BBQs & movie nights, and furnishing the space with very comfortable equipment (think comfy chairs rather than plastic folding ones). And, I wanted to mimic many of the co-working space features. After describing such a space, people would initially respond in a somewhat cynical manner until I described why I wanted these features - we need them in order to both attract and ensure that people come back. We need people to want to be there and turn it into a habit. If they develop a craving to be there, they will come again and again allowing us to more easily get their data.

Until I had read Charles Duhigg’s book The Power of Habit: Why We Do What We Do in Life and Business, I was always having to give this long description. Then I came across his reference to a YMCA study about retention of their members. Although their management had thought that fancy exercise equipment and sparkling, modern facilities would retain members, these features only enticed members join. Rather, it was the need to fill “social habits” that kept members coming back. Members were “driven by emotional factors, such as whether employees knew members’ names or said hello when they walked in. People, it turns out, often go to the gym looking for a human connection, not a treadmill. If a member made a friend at the YMCA, they were much more likely to show up for workout sessions.” If the YMCA satisfied these social needs, members were happy. It needed to be Social. And, that is what caught my attention. In order to keep responders continually coming to an information centre in a crisis, it needs to be Social. It’s the staff, it’s the environment and it’s the services.

Existing models such as the HIC, the FEMA Innovation Team in Sandy, the Humanitarian Information Coordination Cell (as proposed is Disaster Relief 2.0), and co-working spaces could be modified to incorporate the necessary social aspects.  Yes, existing partners might be asked to consider changing the services they provide, but I suspect that groups like the International Humanitarian Partnership and Emergency.lu would be quite interested. New partnerships would need to be found to provide some of the newer social-related services (e.g. coffee organization, furniture organization, etc).

It might see a bit far fetched for the early days of an emergency.  But, how much would you enjoy a free early morning espresso with breakfast before starting a hectic day, a frappucino in the heat of the afternoon, a drink with a free BBQ in the evening, or a hot chocolate while watching a movie with friends on a big screen at the end of a crazy day.

If we could deliver this experience in an emergency, it would provide a short reprieve for a responder and make them feel more supported in countless ways.  And, the relationships developed at the time would carry on well into the future enabling more and more collaboration in emergencies to come.

I can’t wait until someone steps up to this challenge.

Andrej
